relationship-repair-coach.title: Make a Specific Repair Attempt After a Workable Conflict
relationship-repair-coach.subtitle: Own your part, offer a concrete repair, and leave room for the other person's response
relationship-repair-coach.description: After a misunderstanding or conflict where it is safe to re-engage, make a specific repair attempt: name what you did, acknowledge the likely impact without arguing about intent, apologize for your part, offer a concrete corrective action, and invite the other person's view. Do not demand forgiveness or immediate reconciliation.
relationship-repair-coach.reason: Replace an inherited apology-and-forgiveness routine containing invented sincerity percentages, arbitrary timers and targets, and an implicit expectation that the harmed person should forgive. Experimental evidence supports apology as a causal signal that can promote forgiveness, and a large meta-analysis identifies apology and empathy as important correlates of forgiveness. The public protocol therefore focuses on accountable repair while preserving the other person's right not to forgive, reconcile, or continue the relationship.

lifeOsSource.hack: When a conflict is workable and it is safe to re-engage, make one accountable repair attempt rather than trying to win the argument again.
lifeOsSource.whatYouDo: Wait until you can speak without escalating. Name the specific action or words you are taking responsibility for. Acknowledge the impact as you understand it without using your intention to cancel the other person's experience. Apologize for your part without an 'if'. Offer one concrete repair or behavior change you can actually make, then ask how the other person sees it. Listen to the answer. Do not require forgiveness, agreement, or immediate trust in return.
lifeOsSource.checkIn: Did I own a specific part without defending it, offer a realistic repair, and give the other person room to respond or decline?
lifeOsSource.reference: Forster et al. (2021) — randomized experimental evidence on apology, relationship value and forgiveness

references.title: Experimental evidence that apologies promote forgiveness by communicating relationship value
references.claim_scope: Controlled experiments found that apologies can causally promote forgiveness through a pathway shared with perceived relationship value. This supports apology as one useful repair signal; it does not show that apology guarantees forgiveness, restores trust, or resolves every kind of conflict.

references.title: The road to forgiveness: a meta-analytic synthesis of its situational and dispositional correlates
references.claim_scope: Across 175 studies and 26,006 participants, apology and state empathy were among the notable situational correlates of interpersonal forgiveness. The synthesis is primarily about forgiveness correlates, not a validated universal conflict-repair script.

faq.question: What makes an apology useful here?
faq.answer: Keep it specific and accountable. Name what you did, apologize for your part, and offer a concrete repair or change. Avoid conditional wording such as 'I'm sorry if you were hurt' when you already know which behavior caused the problem.

faq.question: What if the other person does not forgive me?
faq.answer: They do not owe forgiveness, reconciliation, or immediate trust. A repair attempt is an action you control; their response is not. Respect a request for time, distance, or a boundary and let future behavior carry more weight than repeated pressure for closure.

faq.question: Should I explain what I intended?
faq.answer: You can clarify intent if it genuinely helps understanding, but do not use intent to erase impact. Start with the part you can own. If your explanation becomes a new argument about why the other person should not feel hurt, the repair attempt has probably drifted back into defense.

faq.question: Is this appropriate after abuse, threats, coercion, or stalking?
faq.answer: No generic repair script should take priority over safety. In abusive, coercive, threatening, or otherwise unsafe situations, distance, boundaries, documentation, and appropriate outside support may be more important than re-engagement. Brali does not treat apology as a safety plan.

intro.html: After an ordinary conflict, a useful repair attempt is less about finding perfect words than about sending a credible signal: I understand what I did, I am willing to own my part, and I am willing to change something concrete. Experimental research shows that apologies can promote forgiveness, while broader evidence links apology and empathy with forgiveness across many studies. That does not make forgiveness mandatory, and it does not turn apology into a reset button for trust.

sections.title: 1. First decide whether repair is the right goal
sections.html: Use this protocol for a workable misunderstanding or conflict where re-engagement is reasonably safe. If there is abuse, coercion, threats, stalking, or fear for safety, do not treat a better apology as the main problem to solve. Safety, distance, boundaries, and outside support can take priority.

sections.title: 2. Own one specific action
sections.html: Start with behavior you can actually name: what you said, did, failed to do, or misunderstood. Avoid a global self-attack and avoid a vague apology that makes the other person prove they were hurt. Specific responsibility gives the conversation something concrete to repair.

sections.title: 3. Acknowledge impact without mind-reading
sections.html: State the impact as you understand it, but leave room to be corrected. For example: 'I can see that interrupting you made it harder for you to explain your point.' Do not insist that good intentions cancel the effect of the behavior.

sections.title: 4. Apologize for your part without demanding a result
sections.html: A concise apology can be enough: 'I interrupted you and dismissed the point before I understood it. I'm sorry for that.' The purpose is to take responsibility, not to extract 'it's okay', forgiveness, or immediate reassurance.

sections.title: 5. Offer one concrete repair or behavior change
sections.html: Ask what can be repaired now and name what you can change next time. Keep the promise small enough to observe. Replacing a grand promise with one specific behavior makes future evidence of change possible.

sections.title: 6. Invite the other person's version and listen
sections.html: Ask how they saw the event or what would help, then listen without immediately correcting every detail. You can disagree with parts of their interpretation and still learn what landed badly. If they want time or distance, that response is part of the information you need to respect.

sections.title: 7. Let later behavior do the rest
sections.html: An apology is one repair signal, not proof that trust has been restored. Repeated behavior matters. Do not keep repeating the apology to pressure the other person into closure. Make the promised change, respect boundaries, and allow reconciliation, if any, to develop on its own timetable.
